# **Nov 17 Was a Fire Drill**

Target length: 9 to 11 minutes. Tone: calm, honest, zero hype. Lines in [brackets] are notes to you, not spoken on camera.

---

## **Part 1: Hook (0:00 to 0:45)**

The blackout everyone warned you about? It didn't happen.

The lights stayed on. Your phone still works. The grocery store is still open.

So a lot of people are going to laugh this off. "See? Fear-mongering. Nothing happened."

But here's what DID happen this week. People across the country couldn't get into their bank accounts. A global Microsoft outage knocked businesses offline. Flights got snarled.

None of that was the power grid. And it still stopped people cold.

I spent 18 years as a firefighter and EMT. And I'm going to tell you why November 17th wasn't a false alarm. It was a fire drill. And most people failed it.

Stick with me. By the end of this video, you'll know the three things you should really be watching right now, and exactly what to do about them. No panic. Just a plan.

---

## **Part 2: Story (0:45 to 3:00)**

Let's clear up what actually happened, because there was a lot of noise.

On November 17th, FEMA and the FCC ran a test of the Emergency Alert System. That's the beep and the message that comes across your radio and TV. [If it was moved: "It got pushed to December 3rd."] It was a test of the warning system. It had nothing to do with power plants, power lines, or your electricity.

These tests aren't random. Federal law requires FEMA to run a national test at least once every three years. The last one was in 2023. If you're over 40, you remember them being a regular thing on TV.

So where did the "90-day blackout" come from?

This fall, the Pentagon rolled out a readiness plan. Part of it says every military department should be able to run on its own for at least 90 days. Its own water. Its own power. Its own fuel. Its own communications.

People saw "90 days" and "military" and decided a blackout was coming. Add a viral post claiming The Simpsons predicted it, and you've got a panic.

But here's the part nobody wants to talk about. The military isn't planning for 90 days because they know a date. They're planning for 90 days because they know the grid can be hit. By weather. By sabotage. By a cyberattack. And they know it can take a long time to fix.

That's not a conspiracy. That's just good planning.

So here's my question for you. The Pentagon is preparing for 90 days. How many days could your family make it right now? Three? One? Be honest.

That's the real lesson of November 17th. Not that nothing happened. It's that for two weeks, a whole lot of people asked themselves, "Would I be ready?" And a lot of them didn't like the answer.

In the fire service, we run drills when nothing is on fire. That's the whole point. You find out what you don't know while it's still cheap to learn it. We had a saying: practice the way you play, and play the way you practice.

So let's learn it. Here are the three things I'd actually be watching right now.

---

## **Part 3: The 3 Real Threats (3:00 to 8:30)**

### **Threat 1: Winter is the grid's weak spot**

The people who watch over the power grid are called NERC. Every year they publish a report on how ready the grid is for winter.

Last winter, a storm called Fern hit the Midwest, the Northeast, and the South. The head of NERC told Congress it was "a near-miss event." Near miss. That's what we call it in the fire service when something almost went very wrong.

Their review this fall said the grid did better than in past storms. But they also said the margin for error can still shrink fast.

Here's why. Going into last winter, the demand for power went up about twice as fast as new power was added. Data centers, more electric homes, more factories. The grid is being asked to do more every year, and it isn't growing as fast.

And going into last winter, they flagged seven regions at higher risk of running short during extreme cold. Texas. New England. Parts of the West.

[Prop: hold up the NOAA radio.]

So what does that mean for you? It means the most likely blackout isn't an attack. It's a cold snap. And a power outage in a cold snap is dangerous fast.

So the fix is simple. Have a safe way to stay warm when the power is out. And please, do not bring a grill, a camp stove, or a generator inside. Every winter, people die from carbon monoxide trying to stay warm. Get a CO detector with a battery backup. It costs less than a pizza.

### **Threat 2: The grid is hard to fix, not just easy to break**

This is the one most prepping videos skip, and it's the real reason a long outage is possible.

The grid runs on huge transformers. Think of them as the heart of a substation. When one is badly damaged, you can't run to the store for a new one.

In a 2025 industry survey, the average wait to get a power transformer was 128 weeks. That's almost two and a half years. Analysts at PwC say some of the largest ones now take up to four years. And prices have jumped about 77 percent since 2019.

Why? AI data centers and new power projects are buying them up faster than factories can build them.

So picture this. A storm, a physical attack, or a cyberattack takes out a few key substations. The power company can patch around some damage. But if the spare parts aren't there, some areas could wait a long time.

That's why the military plans for 90 days. Not because they know a date. Because they know the repair line is long.

I'm not telling you this to scare you. I'm telling you because it changes the question. Stop asking, "Will the power go out?" It will. Start asking, "How long could I last if it stayed out?"

### **Threat 3: The real blackout this week was digital**

Here's what I find wild. Everyone was watching the power grid this week. But the outages that actually hit people were digital.

A global Microsoft outage took businesses offline. Flights were disrupted. And on Monday, customers at major banks reported they couldn't get into their accounts.

[Update these with anything new from Tuesday or Wednesday.]

The lights were on. The power was fine. And people still couldn't pay for gas or groceries.

Most of us carry zero cash now. Our cards, our phone wallets, our banking apps, all of it depends on systems we don't control.

[Prop: hold up the cash envelope.]

The fix is simple and cheap. Keep some cash at home in small bills. Ones, fives, tens, twenties. Enough to buy food, gas, and medicine for a week or two. When the card reader is down, small bills are king, because nobody will have change for a hundred.

And write down the phone numbers you'd need on paper. Your doctor. Your pharmacy. Your family. If your phone dies, can you call anyone? Most people can't.

---

## **Part 4: Offer (8:30 to 10:30)**

So here's my advice. Stop prepping for a date. Dates come and go. Prep for a length of time.

Your first goal is two weeks. Not 90 days. Two weeks. That covers almost every winter storm, most cyber outages, and most of what we saw after the big hurricanes. Once you have two weeks, then you build toward 30.

Here's the two-week checklist, in the order I'd buy it:

1. **Water.** At least one gallon per person per day. Two is better if you can swing it. For a family of four, that's 56 gallons minimum.
2. **Safe heat.** Warm sleeping bags and blankets for everyone, plus a battery CO detector. Don't burn anything indoors that isn't built for it.
3. **Medications.** If anyone in your home takes a daily medicine, talk to your doctor about keeping a two-week buffer. This is the one people forget, and it's the one that sends people to the ER.
4. **Cash.** Small bills, enough for a week or two of food, gas, and medicine.
5. **Food you can eat without cooking.** Canned meat, peanut butter, crackers, oatmeal you can soak. And a manual can opener.
6. **Light and a radio.** Flashlights or lanterns for each room, extra batteries, and a hand-crank or battery NOAA weather radio. When cell towers go down, the radio still works.
7. **A real first aid kit.** Not a 300-piece box of bandaids. I'll do a whole video on building one that fits your family.

[Prop: open the jump kit for a quick look.]

You don't need to buy all of it this week. If money is tight, add one item every payday. That's how real people do it.

Now I want to hear from you. Drop a comment with one number: how many days could your family make it right now, honestly? No judgment. That number is your starting line.

[Offer: point to your free two-week checklist, or your next video. Example: "I put this whole checklist on one page you can print and stick on your fridge. The link is in the description."]

And if you want the next video, subscribe. Next up, I'm covering how to heat your home with no power without putting your family at risk, because that's the one that kills people every winter.

November 17th was a drill. The next one might not be. Let's be ready.

[END]
